6.7 Asset Allocation

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Stage 4 covered the theory of portfolios, capital market assumptions and lifecycle allocation. This lesson turns them into an allocation plan a household can carry out.

Strategic and tactical allocation

Section titled “Strategic and tactical allocation”

Strategic asset allocation is the long-term target mix, for example 60% stocks and 40% bonds. It comes from three things: the household’s goals and horizon; the lower of its risk capacity (how large a loss it can bear financially, which depends on human capital, the emergency fund, debts and so on, 6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance) and its risk tolerance (how much fluctuation it can bear psychologically); and estimates of the long-run returns and risks of each asset class (4.11 Capital Market Assumptions). The strategic allocation is written into the investment policy statement (IPS) and does not change with short-term market moves.

Tactical asset allocation is a temporary departure from the strategic mix based on a view of the short-term market, for example cutting stocks when they look expensive. It is in effect market timing, and like other active management it faces the evidence on market efficiency (4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis) and costs (6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing).

Check C1
A young couple says they could accept a 50% fall in their portfolio, but this money is needed in 3 years for a house down payment, and the amount must be there then. In setting the allocation of this money, the main basis should be:
When tolerance and capacity differ, which governs? If stocks are down 30% in 3 years, what happens to the down payment?
How much does long-run expected return matter for money that must be there in 3 years? How much do stock returns swing over that span?

Lifecycle and glide paths

Section titled “Lifecycle and glide paths”

4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory showed that if human capital is bond-like, a young person’s financial assets can hold more stocks, declining with age. The glide path of a target-date fund (target-date fund) standardizes this idea: for example about 90% stocks 40 years before retirement, falling to 40%–50% at retirement. Some funds reach their lowest stock share at the retirement date (“to”), others keep reducing it for some years after retirement (“through”).

A particular household’s path can depart from the standard: people with stable incomes or pensions can hold more stocks; people whose income moves closely with the stock market (for example in finance or technology, with lots of employer stock) should hold fewer; and large falls in the years just before and after retirement matter most, as 6.9 Retirement Planning discusses.

Check C2
Two 40-year-old investors have the same financial assets and the same risk aversion: one is a tenured professor with a pension, the other an investment banker whose income comes mainly from year-end bonuses and company stock. Following lifecycle allocation, whose financial assets suit a higher stock share?
Does understanding markets lower his risk? What happens to his income when stocks fall?
Total wealth includes human capital. Is the risk of their human capital the same?

International diversification

Section titled “International diversification”

By market value, US stocks make up more than 60% of the global stock market (MSCI ACWI Index, 2025), yet US investors often keep most or even all of their stocks in the US; this is called home bias. The market portfolio of theory (market portfolio) is global.

Correlations between national stock markets have been fairly high since 2000, so international diversification does little to reduce short-term volatility. Its value shows more over the long run: a single country can go through very long slumps; for example the Nikkei 225’s peak of December 1989 was not surpassed until February 2024. Holding foreign assets also brings exchange-rate risk (2.7 The Open Economy): for stocks, currency moves are a small part of total volatility and are usually left unhedged; for bonds, currency moves can be larger than the bonds’ own volatility and are usually hedged (currency hedging). Some common target-date funds hold about 40% of their stocks outside the US.

Check C3
A US investor holds only an S&P 500 index fund. Since these large companies do business worldwide and earn much of their revenue abroad, he is already internationally diversified and needs no stocks outside the US.
Is earning revenue abroad the same as returns coming from a market? If valuations across the US market fell, what would happen to these companies' share prices?

Rebalancing

Section titled “Rebalancing”

Because assets earn different returns, a portfolio drifts away from its targets. Rebalancing means selling assets whose weight is too high and buying those whose weight is too low, bringing the portfolio back to its targets. There are two common rules: rebalance on a calendar (for example once a year), or rebalance when a weight strays more than a set amount from its target (a band rule, for example ±5 percentage points).

Check C4
In Figure 4-1, narrow the rebalancing band from ±5 to ±1 percentage point. Which statement is correct?
Look at the number of rebalances in the readout. What does each rebalance mean in a taxable account?
Look at the readout: how many rebalances are there at ±5 and at ±1?

Rebalancing has costs too: trading costs, and in taxable accounts capital gains tax on selling appreciated assets (6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US)). In practice these can be reduced: use new contributions, dividends and interest to buy the assets that are underweight; make the adjustments in tax-deferred accounts; trade only when the drift is large.

Check C5
A household's stock weight has drifted from its 60% target to 66%. Most of its stocks are in a taxable account with large unrealized gains; its 401(k) holds both stocks and bonds and receives new money every month. The most tax-efficient way to rebalance is:
What does selling stocks with large gains in a taxable account cost? Is trading inside a 401(k) taxed?
Does trading inside a 401(k) create tax? What about using new contributions to buy the underweight asset?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The strategic allocation is the long-term target mix, set by goals, the lower of risk capacity and tolerance, and capital market assumptions; tactical allocation is short-term timing.
  • Glide paths reduce the stock share with age; a particular household should adjust for the nature of its human capital.
  • The US is more than 60% of the global stock market; the benefit of international diversification shows mainly over the long run; foreign stocks are usually unhedged and foreign bonds usually hedged.
  • Rebalancing brings the portfolio back to its targets, on a calendar or by bands; cash flows and tax-deferred accounts reduce its costs.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A 500,000 dollar portfolio starts the year at 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Over the year stocks rise 30% and bonds fall 5%.
(a) What is the stock weight at year end? How many stocks must be sold to return to 60/40 (thousand dollars)?
(b) A friend says: "Rebalancing sells winners and buys losers, and stocks have momentum (4.6 Multifactor Models), so rebalancing lowers returns and should be avoided." Evaluate this statement. Consider a simplified example: one asset first rises 50% and then falls by a third (back to its starting price), and the other is cash earning 0; compare holding 50/50 rebalanced each period with starting at 50/50 and never adjusting, and find each one's growth after two periods. What does the example show? In what kind of market does rebalancing earn less?
Question 2
US stocks have a volatility of 16%, developed markets outside the US 18%, and their correlation is 0.8.
(a) What is the volatility of a stock portfolio of 60% US and 40% international? How much lower than 100% US?
(b) An investor concludes: "International stocks hardly reduce risk and are more volatile, so there is no point in holding them." Evaluate this statement.
Question 3
An investor's strategic allocation is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. CAPE is now high, and using the building-block method (4.11 Capital Market Assumptions) he estimates stocks will return only 5% a year over the next 10 years, and bonds 4%.
(a) By this estimate, what are the expected returns of 60/40 and 30/70?
(b) He plans to "cut stocks to 30% until valuations come down, then add them back". Evaluate this plan. If his estimate of stocks' expected return really has fallen, what would a reasonable adjustment look like?
Question 4
A household's portfolio is 1 million dollars with a 60% stock target. Stocks are now 70%, so about 100,000 dollars of stocks must be sold. In their taxable account the stocks' cost basis is only half their market value; the long-term capital gains rate is 15%. Their 401(k) holds 200,000 dollars, all in stocks.
(a) If they sell 100,000 dollars of stocks in the taxable account, how much tax is due (thousand dollars)?
(b) A friend says: "A rule is a rule; every year every account must be put back to 60/40." Evaluate this statement and give a better rebalancing plan.
